screens.body:
Your machine runs hundreds of processes but has limited RAM. How does everything fit? The OS cheats — brilliantly.

Each process gets its own private address space: it believes it owns all the memory. The OS quietly maps those private addresses onto real RAM behind the scenes.

options: It shares one address with everyone
check.question: Each process believes…

screens.heading: Too many programs, too little RAM
screens.keyPoint: Every process gets a private illusion of full memory.

screens.body:
Virtual memory is that illusion: every process sees a clean, private, continuous stretch of memory. The OS translates each virtual address to a physical one.

This gives you isolation (processes can't peek at each other) and flexibility (a process can use more memory than physically exists, up to a point).

options: A private illusion of its own full memory
check.question: Virtual memory gives each process…

screens.heading: Virtual memory
screens.keyPoint: Virtual addresses map to physical RAM behind the scenes.

screens.body:
The OS chops memory into fixed-size chunks called pages (often 4 KB). A page table maps each virtual page to a physical page — or notes that it's not in RAM right now.

Fixed-size pages make allocation simple: no awkward gaps, no Tetris. Any free page fits any virtual page.
screens.heading: Paging: memory in fixed chunks
screens.keyPoint: Fixed-size pages make memory allocation simple.

screens.body:
Sometimes a program touches a page that isn't in RAM — maybe it was moved to disk. The hardware raises a page fault, and the OS loads the page back in.

Page faults are normal, not errors. But each one costs time, so too many means your program slows down noticeably.

options: The needed page wasn't in RAM, so the OS loads it
check.question: A page fault means…

screens.heading: Page faults
screens.keyPoint: Page faults are normal — but too many slow you down.

screens.body:
When RAM fills up, the OS moves idle pages to disk — that's swapping. It frees RAM, at the cost of slower access later.

Push it too far and you get thrashing: the OS spends all its time swapping pages instead of running programs. Everything crawls. The fix is simple but annoying: close things, or add RAM.

options: The OS swapping so much that nothing gets done
check.question: Thrashing is…

screens.heading: Swapping and thrashing

screens.body:
Before paging, memory was handed out in variable-sized blocks — which left Swiss-cheese gaps (fragmentation) that wasted RAM.

Fixed-size pages dodge most fragmentation: any free page fits anywhere. Simple, predictable, and the reason modern systems all page.
screens.heading: Why paging beats the alternative
screens.keyPoint: Fixed sizes dodge the fragmentation problem.

screens.body:
Ever had 40 browser tabs open and everything slows to a crawl? That's swapping and page faults in action.

And Node.js has a heap limit (a few GB by default) — your backend literally runs inside a virtual address space the OS manages. "Out of memory" crashes are memory management saying no.

check.question: 40 slow browser tabs are likely…

screens.keyPoint: Tab overload and heap limits are memory management live.
